metadata.title: Caught by Code.
metadata.note: Weekly update. Narrator Muskan, @HumanitariansAI, banner 'Vendor Intelligence'. ONE insight: don't trust the brief — grade it against the real collected data, in code. An eval harness runs 6 checks per brief at two severity levels, and caught a real bug on the first run. Bookends render (composer/verdict/handoff/outro); body B01-B04 are house-style 4K PIL cards. DOUBLE-CHECK LAW: details from the creator's own change log (6 checks; score-must-match-calculator; dates→signals, dollars→headlines; hard-fail vs warning; competitor-DB-down bug).

beats.narration_text: Hey, I'm Muskan. The file that was supposed to check my briefs was an empty placeholder. This week I filled it. Now code grades every brief before anyone reads it, and it caught a real bug on the first run.

props.command: My brief eval harness is an empty placeholder. Build one that checks every brief against the real collected data — so wrong statements get caught by code, not by me reading.
output: the eval file was a placeholder
caught a real bug on run one

beats.narration_text: The idea is simple. Every brief gets compared against the actual data we collected for that company. Not vibes, not a human skim, code. Before this, the only way to catch a wrong statement was to read it by hand. That's exactly how I found a factual error earlier today.

show.event: brief box and data box appear, checked between

props.caption: grade the brief against the real collected data

beats.narration_text: Six checks run against that data. Required sections present. No generic filler. Empty sections must say UNKNOWN instead of bluffing. Dates and dollar amounts have to trace to a real signal. And the sharp one: the financial score must exactly match our rule-based calculator, so the AI can't quietly swap in its own number.

show.event: the six checks light in order

props.caption: every check runs against the real collected data

beats.narration_text: The checks come at two levels. Hard failures are real defects, the brief is wrong. Warnings are for a human glance, because sometimes the AI correctly adds up a total that doesn't appear word-for-word in any single headline. That's arithmetic, not a lie, so it's flagged, not failed.

props.caption: a defect fails; a judgment call warns

beats.narration_text: And it worked immediately. On the very first run it flagged this: when the competitor database is unreachable, the brief still writes confident text about competitors, out of nothing. A human might read right past that. The harness didn't.

props.caption: found on run one — a human might have missed it

beats.narration_text: The lesson, same as always: don't trust the output, check it against the source, in code. A test that runs on every brief beats a human reading one brief, once.

artifactLines: The eval file was an empty placeholder — now it grades every brief automatically.
Six checks vs the real data: sections, score = calculator, UNKNOWN not bluffing, no filler, dates → signals, dollars → headlines.
Two levels: hard failures are defects; warnings need a human glance.
Caught a real bug on run one: confident competitor text when the competitor DB was down.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take one thing your AI writes and put a check on it, in code. Pick one claim that must trace to real data, a number, a date, a score, and fail the output when it can't. One automated check beats a hundred careful reads.

props.command: Write an automated check for my AI's output: pick one claim that must trace to source data (a number, a date, a score) and fail the output when it can't be traced.

beats.narration_text: Caught by code. More next week. Humanitarians AI.
